Microsoft releases Windows 10 KB5131096 extended security update

Microsoft released the Windows 10 ESU update KB5131096, bringing systems to build 19045.7846 and delivering November 2026 security fixes. It also resolves remaining USB Audio Class 1.0 issues and fixes printer, Remote Desktop, PowerShell signing, and Cuba daylight-saving-time problems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Microsoft released the Windows 10 KB5131096 extended security update, which updates Windows 10 to build 19045.7846 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 to build 19044.7846.
  • 02The update is available through Windows Update for Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC users and users enrolled in the Extended Security Updates program.
  • 03KB5131096 includes November 2026 Patch Tuesday security fixes, which addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities across Microsoft products, including an actively exploited Outlook zero-day flaw.
  • 04The update fixes printer-addition failures, certain Remote Desktop policy and shadow-connection problems, and remaining USB Audio Class 1.0 issues introduced by September 2026 security updates.
  • 05KB5131096 also changes Cuba daylight-saving-time rules and introduces stricter encoding validation for signed PowerShell scripts.

Microsoft released KB5131096, a Windows 10 extended security update containing the November 2026 Patch Tuesday security fixes and several bug fixes. It is available through Windows Update for Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC users and systems enrolled in the Extended Security Updates program. After installation, Windows 10 reaches build 19045.7846, while Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021 reaches build 19044.7846.

The update incorporates fixes from a Patch Tuesday release that addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities across Microsoft products, including an actively exploited Outlook zero-day flaw. It fixes failures when adding Active Directory-published printers, Remote Desktop policy and shadow-connection issues, and remaining USB Audio Class 1.0 problems introduced by the September 2026 security updates. KB5131096 also updates Cuba daylight-saving-time rules and applies stricter encoding validation to signed PowerShell scripts, which may require affected scripts to be saved as valid UTF-8 with a byte order mark and signed again.

  • Organizations using signed PowerShell scripts should check them for invalid UTF-8 encoding, because KB5131096 can cause previously accepted scripts to fail signature validation unless they are saved as valid UTF-8 with a byte order mark and signed again.
  • KB5131096 resolves the remaining USB Audio Class 1.0 problems caused by the September 2026 security updates, including devices failing to start with Code 10 errors and unresponsive volume controls.
  • The update changes Cuba time settings for an extended 2026–2027 daylight-saving period, keeping Cuba on UTC-04:00 until November 2027.
  • The update includes security fixes from a Patch Tuesday release that addressed an actively exploited Outlook zero-day flaw, making installation particularly important for eligible Windows 10 systems.

Microsoft released KB5131096, a security update for organizations using Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or people enrolled in Windows 10’s Extended Security Updates program. It includes this month’s security fixes, including protection related to a flaw being actively used in Microsoft Outlook, and fixes problems with some printers, remote computer connections, PowerShell scripts, and USB audio devices. Installing it matters because Windows 10 no longer receives new features, so these continuing security updates are an important way for eligible users to stay protected and keep affected devices working properly.

It is particularly relevant to organizations still running eligible Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC or ESU-enrolled systems, and it includes potentially disruptive PowerShell signature-validation changes.

Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments

Attackers used compromised Qubole AWS IAM credentials to assume trusted cross-account roles at dozens of customer environments, steal secrets, and exfiltrate accessible S3 data. Organizations that granted Qubole access should review CloudTrail activity, revoke sessions, rotate credentials, and tighten or remove unused trust relationships.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A threat actor used compromised IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to access and exfiltrate data from customer AWS environments that trusted the account.
  • 02The campaign ran from October 14 to 26 and affected tens of companies, according to the report and Sentra’s confirmation.
  • 03The attacker retrieved secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, read Lambda environment variables, and used TruffleHog to validate discovered credentials.
  • 04After assuming trusted roles, the attacker enumerated accessible S3 buckets and downloaded data from all reachable buckets.
  • 05Potentially affected administrators are advised to review CloudTrail from October 1, rotate exposed credentials, revoke active role sessions, and restrict or remove unused integrations.

A threat actor used compromised AWS IAM credentials associated with Qubole’s AWS account to access multiple customer AWS environments. The campaign ran between October 14 and 26 and affected tens of companies whose cross-account roles trusted Qubole’s account. Sentra confirmed dozens of victims, and reported that millions of files were stolen from one customer alone.

The attackers assumed customer roles, surveyed cloud resources, collected secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and SSM Parameter Store, and read AWS Lambda environment variables. They used TruffleHog to validate discovered AWS keys, Microsoft Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials, then enumerated and downloaded data from accessible Amazon S3 buckets. Potentially affected organizations are advised to review CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward, investigate secret and S3 access, rotate exposed credentials, revoke active role sessions, and restrict or remove unused third-party access.

  • The attackers abused customer roles that had been configured to trust Qubole’s AWS account even though the roles were otherwise unused, showing that dormant third-party access can remain a viable entry point.
  • The data theft was opportunistic: the attacker first checked which S3 buckets each assumed role could access and then downloaded all reachable data rather than targeting identified files.
  • The attacker collected passwords and keys at a reported rate of 100 secrets in seven minutes, making rapid credential rotation and session revocation particularly important after suspicious activity is found.
  • The article recommends reviewing CloudTrail records beginning October 1, earlier than the reported October 14–26 campaign window, to identify potentially related access.

Hackers used stolen access to Qubole, a company that helps businesses process and analyze data in Amazon’s cloud, to enter the cloud accounts of companies that had authorized Qubole to connect. Dozens of companies may have been affected, and the attackers searched for passwords and other login information before downloading files from accessible data-storage areas. This shows how one compromised service provider can put many customers at risk when it has permission to access their systems.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an active, high-impact cross-account cloud breach affecting dozens of organizations, with attackers stealing secrets and accessible S3 data through compromised Qubole AWS credentials. It provides concrete detection and containment actions for organizations that trusted Qubole’s AWS account.

Ransomware recovery is now a client retention metric

Kaseya argues that ransomware recovery success for MSPs depends not only on restoring systems but also on timely client communication, coordinated workflows and transparent billing to preserve trust and renewals. The sponsored article promotes its Trifecta platform as a way to integrate RMM, PSA and backup/recovery operations.
KEY POINTS
  • 01The article argues that a technically successful ransomware recovery can still damage an MSP-client relationship when updates are delayed or recovery charges are unclear.
  • 02It cites industry reports stating that 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within one day, while 55% recovered within a week.
  • 03The article cites Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report, which found that 12% of MSPs lost clients after security incidents.
  • 04It identifies disconnected backup, monitoring, ticketing, and billing tools as causes of slower recovery, broken handoffs, inconsistent client updates, and untracked labor.
  • 05The sponsored article promotes Kaseya Trifecta as a platform that connects RMM, PSA, and BCDR workflows to improve recovery coordination, billing accuracy, and client communication.

The article argues that ransomware recovery for managed service providers (MSPs) is not complete when systems and data are restored. Clients also expect timely updates, a clear explanation of recovery work, and transparent emergency charges. Delayed communication or unexplained costs can damage trust and affect contract renewals even after a technically successful recovery.

It cites industry figures that 16% of affected organizations fully recovered within a day and 55% recovered within a week, while Kaseya’s 2026 Cybersecurity Outlook report found that 12% of MSPs lost clients after security incidents. The article identifies disconnected backup, monitoring, ticketing, and billing tools as sources of slow handoffs, fragmented incident information, inconsistent updates, and untracked labor. It recommends tracking time to the first client update, time to restore critical systems, and time to invoice, and promotes Kaseya Trifecta as a platform that connects RMM, PSA, and backup and disaster recovery workflows.

  • Client retention can be affected by the recovery experience itself, because delayed updates and unexplained emergency charges may undermine trust even after systems are restored.
  • The article identifies three operational measures that expose recovery-process gaps: time to first client update, time to restore critical systems, and time to send an accurate invoice.
  • Tracking labor and restore work during an incident is presented as a way to avoid a choice between absorbing unrecorded costs and sending clients invoices they do not recognize.
  • A single incident record can make client communications more consistent by giving every team member the same information about affected and restored systems.

The article says that after a ransomware incident, a company’s outside technology provider must do more than restore locked or unavailable data and systems. Clients can lose trust when updates are delayed or emergency costs are unclear, even if their business is eventually brought back online. It argues that providers should keep recovery work, client updates, and billing connected so clients understand what is happening and are more likely to keep using the provider.

SAP patches ICM2SHELL and PROXYGATE maximum severity flaws

SAP’s November 2026 updates fix four CVSS 10.0 flaws in NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway that could let unauthenticated remote attackers fully compromise SAP systems. Organizations should urgently apply patches for the ICM2SHELL and PROXYGATE issues.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SAP’s November 2026 security updates patch 35 vulnerabilities, including four flaws rated 10 out of 10 in NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway software.
  • 02The four maximum-severity issues include CVE-2026-76964, CVE-2026-120017, CVE-2026-89103, and CVE-2026-89126, which SAP says unauthenticated attackers can exploit remotely to fully compromise affected systems.
  • 03Onapsis calls CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 ICM2SHELL, and identifies CVE-2026-89103 as the pre-authentication remote-code-execution issue PROXYGATE.
  • 04SAP Gateway enables external applications to connect to SAP backend systems, while SAP Web Dispatcher is widely deployed as a load balancer and reverse proxy in enterprise SAP environments.
  • 05CISA has listed 14 SAP security flaws as actively exploited since November 2021, including three that ransomware groups abused in the wild.

SAP’s November 2026 security updates address 35 vulnerabilities, including four maximum-severity flaws in NetWeaver Application Server ABAP, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway. SAP rated CVE-2026-76964, CVE-2026-120017, CVE-2026-89103, and CVE-2026-89126 at 10 out of 10, stating that unauthenticated attackers could remotely fully compromise affected systems. The issues include memory corruption, missing authentication, and broken access control weaknesses.

Onapsis, which reported three of the flaws, calls CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89126 ICM2SHELL and calls the CVE-2026-89103 pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaw PROXYGATE. According to Onapsis, ICM2SHELL can turn routine web traffic into an entry point for remote code execution without an SAP user, password, or user interaction, while PROXYGATE can make SAP Gateway treat an external attacker as an internal application server. Successful exploitation could expose business data, undermine transaction integrity, and disrupt critical business applications; CISA has identified 14 SAP flaws as actively exploited since November 2021, including three used by ransomware groups.

  • The ICM2SHELL issues affect network-facing components that process routine web traffic, making them particularly consequential because exploitation requires no SAP account, password, or user interaction.
  • PROXYGATE allows an external unauthenticated attacker to impersonate an internal application server to SAP Gateway, potentially gaining control under the account that owns the SAP installation.
  • The affected Web Dispatcher component is deployed in almost every enterprise SAP environment and serves as both a load balancer and reverse proxy, which broadens the potential relevance of CVE-2026-89126.
  • These patches continue a recent run of maximum-severity SAP fixes, including an August Commerce Cloud flaw that was reportedly targeted in attacks days after its patch was released.
  • SAP’s track record of 14 flaws listed by CISA as actively exploited since November 2021, with three abused by ransomware groups, underscores the real-world importance of promptly addressing SAP security updates.

SAP released fixes for 35 security problems, including four critical weaknesses in software used by businesses to run and connect important company systems. Without these fixes, an outsider could potentially take full control of affected SAP systems without needing a username or password. This could expose business data, alter transactions, or disrupt essential operations at organizations that use SAP’s NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, or Gateway software.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

SAP patched four CVSS 10.0 flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote compromise of NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, and Gateway systems. The affected components are central to enterprise SAP environments, and the issues require no SAP credentials or user interaction.

Google patches eighth Chrome zero-day exploited in attacks this year

Google released emergency Chrome updates for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free flaw in the browser’s XML component that is already being exploited in the wild. Users should update Chrome immediately, as this is the eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day patched by Google in 2026.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Google released emergency Chrome security updates for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free flaw in Chrome’s XML component that is being exploited in the wild.
  • 02Google said it is restricting bug details and links until most users have received the fix, and may retain restrictions when an affected third-party library remains unpatched in other projects.
  • 03The fixes are rolling out through Chrome’s Stable Desktop channel for Windows, macOS versions 157.0.8103.50/.51, and Linux version 157.0.8103.50.
  • 04CVE-2026-125350 is the eighth Chrome zero-day Google has patched in 2026 after evidence of active exploitation.
  • 05Chrome can install the update automatically after the browser is next launched, or users can manually check for updates.

Google released emergency Chrome security updates for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity flaw in the browser’s XML component that is being exploited in the wild. The issue is a use-after-free weakness, in which Chrome’s XML parser deletes an object from memory but does not clear the reference to it. An attacker could exploit the resulting memory corruption when the browser later accesses that freed memory, potentially manipulating memory and running malicious code.

The fixes are rolling out through Chrome’s Stable Desktop channel for Windows, macOS versions 157.0.8103.50/.51, and Linux version 157.0.8103.50. Google said distribution could take days or weeks, but the update was available when BleepingComputer checked, and Chrome can also install it automatically after the next launch. This is the eighth Chrome zero-day patched in 2026 after evidence that attackers were actively exploiting it, following earlier flaws affecting components including V8, Skia, Dawn, and CSS font features.

  • The update was available immediately when BleepingComputer checked, even though Google said the wider rollout could take days or weeks, so users can manually check rather than wait for the automatic rollout.
  • This year’s actively exploited Chrome flaws have affected several distinct browser components, including XML processing, CSS font features, graphics rendering, WebGPU, and the V8 JavaScript engine.
  • Google is withholding technical details about the flaw while users update, a measure it says may also remain in place if an affected third-party library is still unpatched elsewhere.
  • Chrome users can receive the fix without manually downloading anything because the browser is designed to install updates after its next launch.

Google released an emergency update for Chrome after finding that attackers are already using a flaw in the browser. The problem could let a malicious website interfere with the browser’s memory and potentially run harmful code on a person’s computer. Chrome users on Windows, macOS, and Linux are affected and should update, because this is the eighth Chrome flaw known to have been used in real attacks this year.

Hackers now exploit critical Barracuda ESG flaws to gain root access

Barracuda warns that attackers are actively exploiting two recently patched flaws in its Email Security Gateway, which can be chained to bypass authorization and execute commands as root. Organizations should immediately apply patches and restrict Admin UI access to trusted internal networks.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Barracuda warned that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, two recently patched flaws affecting its Email Security Gateway products.
  • 02CVE-2026-116606 can allow modification of an appliance's global configuration, while CVE-2026-111560 allows unauthenticated OS command injection with root privileges.
  • 03Barracuda said successful exploitation requires access to an affected device's administrative interface, and chaining the flaws can bypass authorization controls and provide root access.
  • 04The company identified exploitation affecting a small number of organizations and urged customers to apply patches immediately or enable automatic patching.
  • 05CVE-2026-111560 also affects Barracuda Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway products.

Barracuda Networks warned that attackers are actively exploiting two recently patched vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway (ESG) appliances: CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560. Barracuda said it has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations. The company urged customers to apply the relevant patches immediately and recommended enabling automatic patching where it has been disabled.

CVE-2026-116606 is an authentication weakness that can let an attacker alter an appliance’s global configuration, while CVE-2026-111560 allows unauthenticated operating-system command injection with root privileges. Barracuda said attacks require access to the affected device’s administrative interface, and that using the flaws together can bypass authorization controls and give an attacker root access. The command-injection issue also affects Barracuda Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway products, while the ESG is affected by both flaws.

  • The risk is especially severe when the two flaws are used together, because one can bypass authorization controls while the other enables commands to run with the device's highest level of access.
  • Although the main Email Security Gateway is affected by both flaws, several other Barracuda products are affected only by the command-injection flaw, making patching relevant beyond email-security appliances.
  • Barracuda said exploitation requires access to the administrative interface, so limiting that interface to trusted internal networks is a stated mitigation alongside installing patches.
  • Barracuda's warning follows prior zero-day campaigns against its Email Security Gateway, including activity that the company said lasted at least seven months and involved data theft from compromised devices.

Barracuda says attackers are using two newly fixed weaknesses in some of its security devices to take full control of them. The issue affects a small number of organizations so far, but customers using the affected email, web, load-balancing, and message-archiving products should install the available updates quickly. Full control of these devices could let attackers bypass protections and access information handled by the organization.

Turla hackers use new Cereal malware to spy on govt Exchange servers

Russia-linked Turla used its new Cereal malware framework to quietly spy on emails at government Microsoft Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania, including correspondence involving NATO and the EU. The toolset hides inside legitimate Exchange processes, selectively collects messages and attachments, and executes commands without external command-and-control infrastructure.
KEY POINTS
  • 01ESET identified Turla's Cereal malware toolset on Microsoft Exchange servers at a government organization in Kazakhstan in late 2025 and at a Romanian government agency compromised on December 23, 2025.
  • 02Turla used the CerealBox component to run inside Exchange's EdgeTransport.exe process and intercept email handling without registering a new email-processing component or disrupting delivery.
  • 03The malware was configured to selectively collect emails with DOC, DOCX, or PDF attachments and to match specified sender, recipient, and subject criteria.
  • 04CerealNeuron accepted encrypted web requests disguised as legitimate Exchange services, executed supplied programs in memory, and encrypted their output for return to the attackers.
  • 05ESET observed no external command-and-control infrastructure in the campaign, with the compromised Exchange server serving as the attackers' only control point.

ESET documented a late-2025 cyberespionage campaign in which the Russia-linked Turla group used a new toolset called Cereal against Microsoft Exchange servers at government organizations. The researchers first found the malware at a government body in Kazakhstan, then identified the same toolset at a Romanian government agency compromised on December 23, 2025. In Romania, the attackers selectively collected correspondence involving representatives of NATO and the European Union.

CerealBox injects into Exchange’s EdgeTransport.exe process and takes over existing email-handling functions, allowing it to inspect selected messages without registering a new transport agent or disrupting mail delivery. It can target messages based on sender, recipient, subject, and attached DOC, DOCX, or PDF files. Another component, CerealNeuron, receives encrypted commands through Exchange-like web paths, executes programs in memory, and returns encrypted results; ESET observed no external command-and-control infrastructure, with the compromised Exchange server serving as the attackers’ only control point.

  • Cereal can inspect email content while avoiding the creation of a new Exchange transport agent, helping it blend into normal server operation without interrupting mail delivery.
  • The attackers used the compromised Exchange server itself as their control point rather than relying on external command-and-control infrastructure, reducing a common opportunity for defenders to detect or block communications.
  • ESET found numerous near-identical command-carrying programs compiled for specific tasks, which it says strongly suggests Turla has an internal system for automating command compilation and packaging.
  • A CerealNeuron variant named CerealHermit can read encrypted commands from files on the server rather than receiving them over the network, providing a possible alternative if the web-based command channel is unavailable.

A Russia-linked spying group called Turla used a new tool named Cereal to secretly read selected emails on Microsoft Exchange email servers used by government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania. In Romania, it targeted messages involving NATO and the European Union, including emails with documents attached. This matters because the tool is designed to stay hidden for a long time while giving attackers access to sensitive government communications, potentially affecting diplomatic and national-security matters.

This is a significant report on an active, Russia-linked Turla cyberespionage campaign targeting government Microsoft Exchange servers in Kazakhstan and Romania. It provides concrete details on a new stealthy toolset, targeted email collection, and techniques that can help defenders investigate Exchange environments.

A critical Xen Orchestra authentication bypass flaw, VSA-2026-062, is being actively exploited to gain admin access and potentially take over XCP-ng hosts as root. Organizations should immediately update to Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 or 6.10.0 and investigate known indicators of compromise.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Vates says the critical Xen Orchestra authentication bypass vulnerability VSA-2026-062 is being actively exploited.
  • 02Remote attackers with network access to the Xen Orchestra management interface can use a specially crafted authentication cookie containing an empty JSON object to log in as an existing token owner without credentials.

Vates has warned that a critical Xen Orchestra authentication bypass flaw, tracked as VSA-2026-062, is being actively exploited. The issue affects Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance, which are used to manage XCP-ng virtual machines, hosts, and pools. An attacker with network access to the management interface can bypass authentication and gain administrator privileges.

The flaw involves sending a specially crafted authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D cookie containing an empty JSON object, causing Xen Orchestra to retrieve an existing authentication token and log the attacker in as its owner. Attackers can then obtain reusable login token IDs through the /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens API endpoint, and a compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and root-level takeover of XCP-ng nodes. Vates released patched Xen Orchestra versions 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, advises immediate updates, and provided indicators including suspicious cookies, connections, VM settings, and files associated with a known campaign.

  • The crafted authentication cookie can cause Xen Orchestra to retrieve an existing authentication token and log an attacker in as that token’s owner, rather than merely bypassing a single login check.
  • After gaining access, an attacker can retrieve reusable login token IDs from the users/me authentication_tokens API endpoint, enabling continued access.
  • The malicious-cookie activity does not create identifying log entries, so Vates says it must be detected through HTTP monitoring rather than relying on standard host logs.
  • Vates identified unusual VM serial-port settings and specific cron and hidden files as host-level signs of the known campaign, but cautioned that these indicators may not apply to other attackers.

A serious flaw in Xen Orchestra, software used to manage virtual machines and their underlying servers, is already being used by attackers. By sending a specially made website cookie, an attacker who can reach the management page can log in without a password and gain administrator-level control. This could let them run code on managed systems and take full control of XCP-ng servers, so organizations using the affected software should install the available updates immediately and check for signs of compromise.

Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones

Git patched CVE-2026-111760, a flaw that could let a malicious repository execute code during recursive clones by abusing an extremely long path to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symlink to attacker-controlled hooks. Users should update Git and bundled Git distributions promptly, and avoid recursively cloning untrusted repositories until patched.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Git fixed CVE-2026-111760 in Git 2.56.1 and corresponding maintenance releases for versions 2.50 through 2.55.
  • 02The flaw allows a malicious repository with an extremely long path to bypass a safety check and cause Git to write a shortened path name chosen by an attacker, including .git.
  • 03During a recursive clone, an attacker can use the issue to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link to a directory containing malicious hooks or configuration, which can lead to code execution.
  • 04GitHub has applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, while fixed GitHub Enterprise Server versions include 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4.
  • 05Until users install fixed versions, GitHub advises cloning only from trusted servers and avoiding recursive clones, merges, binary patches, and fast-import streams from untrusted sources.

Git released fixes for CVE-2026-111760, a flaw that can allow a malicious repository to run attacker-controlled code when it is recursively cloned along with its submodules. The issue is an integer truncation problem in Git’s index handling: an extremely long repository path can pass a safety check but later be written to disk under a shorter attacker-chosen name, including .git. Git 2.56.1 and maintenance releases for the 2.50 through 2.55 series reject such paths before their lengths can be truncated.

The attack uses submodules because a freshly cloned submodule’s .git is a file, which can be replaced with a symbolic link to a directory containing malicious Git hooks or configuration. GitHub has applied fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and released fixed GitHub Enterprise Server versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. The releases also address five other flaws involving path traversal, a stack-memory corruption denial of service, an out-of-bounds read, heap-memory corruption during large merges, and unsafe fast-import features; until patched, GitHub advises users to avoid untrusted recursive clones, merges, binary patches, and fast-import streams.

  • The recursive-clone flaw depends on submodules because a newly cloned submodule has a .git file, whereas Git will not replace a .git folder with a symbolic link.
  • Updating Git alone may not be sufficient if applications ship their own embedded copy of Git, so those applications also need updated versions.
  • Code-hosting servers may be exposed to the large-merge memory corruption flaw through git merge-tree when checking whether user-submitted pull or merge requests can be merged.
  • Servers that cannot immediately update can mitigate the conflict-marker-size issue by setting conflict-marker-size=7 in each repository’s info/attributes file or by disabling merge checks for untrusted repositories.

Git has fixed a serious flaw that could allow a harmful code project to run an attacker’s commands on someone’s computer when they copy that project together with its linked components. The issue affects people and organizations using older Git versions, including some tools and services that include their own copy of Git. Updating Git is important because attackers could use trusted-looking shared code projects to take control of a developer’s work environment or disrupt code-hosting services.

SAP fixed four vulnerabilities rated CVSS 10.0 during its November Security Patch Day. The flaws affect SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP components, SAP Web Dispatcher, SAP Gateway, and the SAML2 service provider. None requires a user to log in or take action for an attacker to exploit it. SAP strongly recommends applying the relevant security notes as a priority.

Two flaws, CVE-2026-76964 in the Internet Communication Manager and CVE-2026-89126 in Web Dispatcher, involve malformed WebSocket traffic that can corrupt memory and potentially let an attacker run code. CVE-2026-120017 can let an attacker sign in as any user, including privileged users, under certain SAML2 configurations where incoming assertions were not checked for signatures. CVE-2026-89103 can let an external attacker be treated as one of the system’s own application servers through SAP Gateway and take unauthorized actions. RedRays advises organizations to patch kernels and all Web Dispatchers together, review SAML2 and Gateway settings, and ensure affected services are not directly exposed where possible.

  • Patching a Web Dispatcher can temporarily shield an affected Internet Communication Manager only when no one can directly reach the Internet Communication Manager’s network ports.
  • Organizations using SAML2 browser logon for services such as Fiori Launchpad or Web GUI should treat their AS ABAP systems as affected until they confirm otherwise, because the article states there is no workaround for the SAML flaw.
  • For SAP Gateway, the article recommends checking that explicit secinfo and reginfo rules are present and restricting access to the gateway’s 33xx port from user networks and the internet.
  • RedRays recommends updating SAP kernels and all Web Dispatchers together so that a single rollout covers all 17 kernel and Web Dispatcher fixes issued that month.
  • Disabling WebSocket support can block the ICM and Web Dispatcher flaws temporarily, but it may disrupt dependent features including ABAP Push Channels and some Fiori functions.

SAP released fixes for four serious weaknesses in software used to run and connect many SAP business systems. On affected systems, an outsider may be able to take control of a system, sign in as any user, or pretend to be a trusted internal server without needing an account or a person to click anything. SilentDelivery injected obfuscated code into compromised websites and showed selected Windows users a fake Google Chrome certificate warning that urged them to install a supposed Certificate Fix utility, which delivered SquadC or a SparrowDoor variant. OceanGate compromised Linux servers, deployed AnnobinDoor and SparrowShell, harvested credentials, and moved into Windows systems to deploy tools for reconnaissance, keylogging, credential collection, and remote access. DarkWire focused on Latin American telecommunications and government organizations, using DLL sideloading to deploy CopperDoor, CopperDNS, proxy tools, and an LSASS-dumping component while placing tools in existing system paths to reduce its footprint.

  • OceanGate used kernel-level packet interception to make a SparrowDoor backdoor appear to communicate through a legitimate externally available service port, such as port 443, while secretly redirecting selected connections to an internal high-numbered port.
  • DarkWire operators avoided creating new folders and instead placed their tools in existing system paths, reducing obvious traces on compromised machines.
  • CopperDoor command-and-control servers were often hosted on Latin American IP addresses in the same country as the targeted organization, which Check Point said could help malicious traffic blend with normal local network activity.
  • SparrowShell shared code and infrastructure similarities with the previously documented Mélofée Linux malware, raising the possibility that CopperDragon also developed and supplied Mélofée.

Researchers linked three suspected China-connected spying campaigns to a shared set of malicious software tools called Sparrow, believed to be developed by a group they call CopperDragon. The campaigns targeted telecommunications companies, government bodies, military organizations, research institutions, and critical infrastructure in Latin America, Asia, and Europe, using compromised websites, deceptive downloads, and exposed internet-connected servers to gain access. This matters because the attackers can steal passwords and sensitive information, monitor victims, and quietly keep access to important networks while making their activity appear legitimate.

KEY POINTS
  • 01Vates VMS warned that a critical Xen Orchestra authentication-bypass flaw, tracked as VSA-2026-062, is being actively exploited in the wild.
  • 02The flaw allows specially crafted authentication cookies to be treated as an unfiltered token lookup, potentially authenticating an attacker as the owner of a valid token.
  • 03An attacker can use the issue to perform actions with administrator privileges, potentially execute code on managed pools, and take over an XCP-ng node as root.

  • 05Reported indicators of compromise include requests containing authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D or authenticationToken=j:{}, a virtual machine named pivot2, and suspicious cron files or files named .ustar5 and .ustar6.

Vates VMS has warned that attackers are actively exploiting a critical Xen Orchestra authentication-bypass vulnerability tracked as VSA-2026-062. The flaw has no CVE identifier yet. It can allow an unauthenticated attacker to obtain administrator-level access and perform arbitrary actions.

The issue arises because a specially crafted REST cookie, authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D, is parsed as an empty object and used in an unfiltered authentication-token lookup. If the selected token is unexpired, the attacker is authenticated as that token’s owner, and an endpoint can return reusable login token IDs. Vates said this can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and full root-level takeover of XCP-ng nodes.

The company released fixes in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, as well as xo-server 5.211.2 and 5.213.1. Reported indicators include requests containing the crafted token value, a virtual machine named pivot2, certain VM serial settings, and suspicious cron or hidden files. Organizations that cannot patch immediately are advised to avoid exposing Xen Orchestra to the internet, block the cited IP address and Tor domain, filter the empty token pattern, and rotate passwords and secrets if compromise indicators are found.

  • A cookie value that decodes to an empty object can cause Xen Orchestra to select the first unexpired authentication token rather than require a valid token string.
  • After bypassing sign-in, the affected users/me authentication-tokens endpoint can expose reusable login token IDs, allowing continued access beyond the initial crafted request.
  • Organizations unable to patch immediately can reduce exposure by removing Xen Orchestra from the public internet or blocking the empty-token pattern at a web application firewall or reverse proxy.
  • The reported activity includes configuration of virtual machines with the "hvm_serial: file" parameter, in addition to suspicious cron entries and files.

Vates VMS says criminals are actively using a serious flaw in Xen Orchestra, software used to manage XCP-ng computer systems, to get administrator-level access without a valid login. A specially crafted website cookie can make the software accept an attacker as an existing user and reveal reusable sign-in tokens. This could let attackers control managed systems, run their own commands, and ultimately take over affected XCP-ng servers. Organizations using Xen Orchestra should install the available fixes or keep the management software off the public internet while they update.

Beyond the Alert: The Case for Rich Network Data

Corelight argues that effective network incident response depends on rich, searchable network evidence—not just alerts—so analysts and AI can trace activity, validate findings, and understand an attack’s full scope.   • 01The article argues that preventing every security incident is not possible, so teams need to find and disrupt activity that has entered their networks.

  • 03Rich network data can include transaction details, packet content, extracted files, searchable history, and context that allows analysts to follow connections over time.
  • 04AI tools can process large amounts of security data and help investigate unfamiliar services, processes, and log formats, but their outputs still need to be checked against evidence.

The article argues that security prevention has limits and that teams must be able to find and disrupt activity that has already entered a network. Alerts can show that something occurred, but they may not reveal whether an intruder moved to other machines, sought additional access, or explored the environment. The ability to trace that activity is presented as the opportunity to intervene before data is stolen or systems are disrupted.

It distinguishes shallow network data, such as timestamps, IP addresses, and basic connection details, from richer data that preserves transaction detail and context. Richer data can support searches across time and hosts, packet-content review, file extraction, and reconstruction of what occurred before and after an alert. The article also says AI can process data at large scale and assist with unfamiliar information, but analysts must validate AI-generated explanations, queries, scripts, and commands against underlying evidence.

  • A useful product evaluation should deliberately depart from the vendor’s guided demo by asking an unanticipated question and tracing the activity both backward and forward in time.
  • Rich data is presented as valuable not only for finding known threats, but also for helping AI identify subtle patterns across hosts and behaviors that shallow connection summaries cannot correlate.

The article says that a security warning alone is often not enough to show what an intruder did inside a computer network. It argues that security teams need detailed records of network activity so they can trace what happened before and after a warning, determine how far an intruder got, and stop further harm. This matters because automated tools can help review large amounts of information, but people still need clear evidence to check whether those tools are correct and make safe decisions.

NEAR AI said the attacker could potentially have viewed requests processed by that server, including requests sent in confidential mode. Although those requests are processed inside a trusted execution environment intended to keep them private, NEAR AI said that protection does not prevent attacks against vulnerable software running within it.

Blind Eagle, also known as APT-C-36, has launched a phishing campaign against organizations in Latin America using fake judicial and administrative notices in Spanish and Portuguese. The messages target people handling cases, contracts, and institutional service requests and use themes including court notifications, Fiscalía notices, tutela proceedings, and administrative documents. Zenox attributed the activity to a Brazilian operational cluster based on its infrastructure, operating time zone, lures, and regional targeting. Colombia remains a priority target, although the phishing wave was not limited to Colombian organizations.

One identified lure used a weaponized SVG file that displayed a fake Colombian Fiscalía General de la Nación webpage and created a ZIP archive locally in the browser through HTML smuggling. The archive contained a JavaScript dropper posing as Network Configuration Auditor version 2.7.298, which collected system and network details before launching a Visual Basic Script. That script bypassed Windows AMSI and ETW monitoring, displayed a fake criminal-citation page, removed the original XHTML file and Mark of the Web metadata, and established startup-folder persistence. PowerShell then decoded and ran an AsyncRAT fork with DCRat lineage in memory.

The campaign puts sensitive legal, financial, and institutional information at risk because it targets judicial, fiscal, administrative, and educational organizations. Zenox observed nearly 3,300 malicious emails in a targeted wave between late October and early November 2026, but could not confirm successful compromises. The article notes that uneven security maturity in portions of Colombia’s public, financial, critical, and private-sector infrastructure may increase opportunities for compromise, data theft, fund theft, or credential reuse.

  • The JavaScript dropper checks for Portuguese- and Spanish-localized directories while collecting system and network details, indicating that language and regional environment are part of its host profiling.
  • The malware displays a fake criminal-citation page while it disables Windows security monitoring and installs itself to run at startup, combining distraction with persistence.
  • Zenox linked the activity to a Brazilian operational cluster based on its infrastructure, operating time zone, Portuguese and Spanish lures, and regional targeting.
  • The campaign’s focus on judicial, fiscal, administrative, and educational organizations places legal, financial, and institutional information at particular risk.

A group called Blind Eagle is sending fake court, government, and administrative notices in Spanish and Portuguese to organizations in Latin America, especially Colombia. The targets include people handling legal cases, contracts, and public-service requests, putting sensitive legal, financial, and institutional information at risk. France has attributed an October cyberattack affecting refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit it links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The operation caused food losses estimated at several tens of millions of euros and about 20 fires. France called it the first offensive cyber campaign on its soil carried out purely for sabotage. Authorities plan to summon Iran’s ambassador, seek new European sanctions, and pursue international arrest warrants for the unit’s leadership.

Attackers reportedly accessed Danfoss and Dixell refrigeration controllers through internet-facing management interfaces, started abnormal defrost cycles without time limits, and disabled temperature safety alerts. Victims included large retailers such as Casino, Leclerc, Carrefour, and Intermarché, along with smaller butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and food plants. France’s cyber coordination center also linked the campaign’s infrastructure to reconnaissance of Schneider Electric equipment at small energy and water-production sites. CERT-FR advised operators to remove affected controllers from direct internet exposure, review configurations, update firmware, change default passwords, and use secure network access.

  • The sabotage did not require changing the refrigeration hardware itself: attackers used publicly reachable management pages to alter defrost settings and turn off the alarms intended to warn when temperatures became unsafe.
  • France described the incident as its first offensive cyber campaign on French soil conducted purely for sabotage, highlighting that the operation was intended to cause physical and economic harm rather than only collect information.
  • The same infrastructure was used to examine Schneider Electric equipment at small energy and water-production sites, linking the supermarket disruption to interest in other industrial systems.
  • For unsupported refrigeration controllers, CERT-FR warned that a factory reset removes an intruder’s continued access but does not fix the underlying exposure, making renewed compromise highly likely if the device remains online.
  • France’s attribution relied on several combined indicators, including the group’s usual scanning tool, Persian-language traces, Iran-linked IP addresses, a propaganda outlet’s early reporting, and an attack method investigators considered typical of the unit.

France says an Iran-linked group remotely changed settings on refrigeration equipment at about 700 French stores and food businesses, causing spoiled food and around 20 fires. Large retailers as well as small butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and food plants were affected. The case shows that internet-connected equipment used in everyday businesses can be manipulated from afar in ways that cause physical damage, financial losses, and risks to people.

  • 01A trucking company accounting clerk received a fuel-card over-limit notice that used the company name, a same-day national truck-stop purchase, and a reference number.

  • 03The lookalike domain webwexsources[.]com was registered about 27 minutes before the email was sent, but SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication passed because the attacker controlled the sending domain.
  • 04Mailbox filtering initially placed the message in Junk, link scanners marked both links as clean, and a human analyst later quarantined and resolved the incident as malicious.

A trucking company accounting clerk received a fuel-card over-limit notice claiming that a same-day purchase at a national truck-stop chain had pushed the company above its assigned limit. The message included the company name, a reference number, and a warning that further fuel purchases might be declined. It used a display name resembling WEX and was signed “WEX Account Support,” while directing the recipient to a plain-text link.

The link opened a clone of the WEX eManager organization login page with an email field, a Continue button, and a passkey option; a second hostname displayed the same page. The attacker-controlled lookalike domain was registered about 27 minutes before the email was sent, yet SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication passed because the attacker controlled the domain and its records. Link scanners marked the URLs clean, but a human analyst identified the message as malicious, and the article advises finance teams to verify whether the card account and referenced transaction exist by using a bookmarked provider portal rather than an email link.

  • Passing sender-authentication checks did not establish legitimacy because the attacker had registered and configured the domain they used only minutes before sending the email.
  • The message’s operational consequence—fuel purchases potentially being declined—created pressure tailored to a trucking company’s accounting function rather than relying on a generic payment-themed lure.
  • The captured fake login page showed only an email-entry form, so the article distinguishes a confirmed login-page clone from an unobserved later-stage credential capture.
  • The article recommends validating the underlying business claim, such as whether the company has a card account and matching transaction, instead of treating valid email headers as proof that a finance notice is real.

A trucking company’s accounting clerk received a fake warning claiming the company’s fuel card had gone over its limit and that more fuel purchases could be declined. The email used the company’s name, a truck-stop purchase, and a reference number to create urgency, then sent the clerk to a convincing copy of the WEX account login page. Although the email appeared to pass normal sender checks, its web address had been registered only 27 minutes earlier, and a human reviewer identified it as malicious. If someone entered account details on the fake page, criminals could potentially gain access to a fuel-card account and disrupt fuel purchases, deliveries, and payments.

Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday addressed 1,093 CVEs across 287 products and components: 63 critical, 1,029 important, and one moderate. Elevation-of-privilege issues accounted for 48.9% of the fixes, followed by remote-code-execution issues at 27.1%. Microsoft Office Word, Excel, and SQL Server had the largest numbers of CVEs patched, with 65, 64, and 53 respectively.

The moderate Outlook spoofing flaw CVE-2026-124194 was exploited in the wild as a zero-day and can allow an attacker who convinces a person to open a crafted Office file to obtain that person’s NTLMv2 hash for follow-on impersonation. Microsoft also fixed critical remote-code-execution vulnerabilities in Active Directory Domain Services, Exchange Server, and Windows Schannel, each assessed as “Exploitation More Likely.” Other notable more-likely-to-be-exploited issues include flaws in Visual Studio Code, Windows Network Address Translation, Windows Installer, the Windows kernel, and Windows Print Spooler Components.

Microsoft’s advisory credited a security researcher who used Anthropic’s Claude for discovering CVE-2026-124194, without naming the Claude version. The update covers a wide range of Microsoft products, including Windows, Office, Exchange, SharePoint, SQL Server, Azure services, and Visual Studio. Tenable recommends applying patches as soon as possible and regularly scanning environments to find systems that remain unpatched.

  • The only moderate-rated issue, CVE-2026-124194 in Outlook, was already exploited in the wild, showing that severity ratings alone do not identify the most urgent patching priority.
  • Microsoft credited the discovery of CVE-2026-124194 to a researcher using Anthropic’s Claude, although the advisory did not identify a specific Claude version.
  • Several vulnerabilities assessed as “Exploitation More Likely” affect core enterprise services including Active Directory Domain Services, Exchange Server, Schannel, Windows NAT, and Visual Studio Code.
  • Although most fixes were rated important rather than critical, elevation-of-privilege issues made up nearly half of all patched vulnerabilities, at 48.9%.
  • Microsoft SharePoint Server’s CVE-2026-120002 has a CVSSv3 score of 9.9 but is rated important and assessed as “Exploitation Less Likely,” illustrating that the article distinguishes severity scores from expected exploitability.

Microsoft released November 2026 security updates that fix 1,093 weaknesses across Windows, Office, Exchange, SharePoint, SQL Server, and many other Microsoft products. People and organizations using these products could be affected because some flaws could let an attacker take control of a computer, gain greater access, or impersonate a user. One Outlook flaw had already been used in real-world attacks and can expose a user’s login proof after they open a specially made Office file. Installing the updates promptly helps reduce the chance that attackers can use these weaknesses.

Sage: AI for Assumed-Breach Operations, Built Into Mythic

SpecterOps has released Sage, an open-source AI assistant embedded in Mythic v4 that helps operators plan and execute assumed-breach operations across Mythic agents while requiring approval for each action in supervised mode. Sage uses BloodHound and a proof-backed engagement ledger to preserve operational context, with autonomous operation restricted to research labs.
KEY POINTS
  • 01SpecterOps released Sage as an open-source AI assistant that runs inside Mythic v4 and helps operators translate objectives into proposed actions across available Mythic agents.
  • 02Sage offers conversation, supervised, and autonomous modes; supervised mode requires approval for every guarded action, while autonomous mode is described as an experimental research capability for lab environments.
  • 03Sage stores operational context in BloodHound and an Engagement State Ledger, where claimed gains are recorded as achieved only when supported by Mythic, credential, callback, task, file, or BloodHound evidence.
  • 04Sage can learn command schemas from installed Mythic payload types, validate proposed arguments before tasking, and use built-in capabilities that convert selected actions into concrete Mythic commands.
  • 05The project is beta software validated primarily with Mythic v4, LiteLLM, and the Apollo payload, with other providers and Mythic agents supported but not yet fully validated.

SpecterOps has released Sage, an open-source AI assistant that runs as a native chat container inside Mythic v4 for assumed-breach operations. Operators can describe an objective, and Sage identifies suitable Mythic agents, callbacks, commands, and arguments while retaining operator control through approval cards. Sage is intended to reduce the burden of tracking command syntax, tool availability, and operational information across long-running assessments.

Sage provides read-only conversation mode, supervised mode requiring approval for each guarded action, and an experimental autonomous mode intended only for lab use. It maintains operational context through BloodHound attack-path data and an Engagement State Ledger that records gains only when they are supported by evidence from Mythic tasks, files, credentials, callbacks, or BloodHound data. Sage can query installed Mythic agent schemas, validate proposed command arguments, and use programmed capabilities that generate and verify concrete actions; however, it remains beta software, with end-to-end validation primarily conducted using Mythic v4, LiteLLM, and the Apollo payload.

  • Sage separates AI decision-making from command construction for its programmed capabilities: the model selects a capability, while code generates the concrete Mythic commands and verifies their effects against actual output.
  • An entry in Sage’s Engagement State Ledger is not treated as achieved merely because the model says so; it must include a proof record tied to evidence such as Mythic task output, callback records, credentials, files, or BloodHound data.
  • Sage can work with different Mythic agents by querying Mythic’s own command schemas, checking that a command is available on the selected callback, and validating or repairing arguments before presenting an approval request.
  • Autonomous mode does not use the normal multi-agent conversation system; it instead uses a deterministic cycle that evaluates available capabilities, verifies results, and stops under limits for cycles, lack of progress, tokens, or elapsed time.
  • The article cites prior research indicating that language models handle individual penetration-testing tasks better than sustained multi-host operations, which is why Sage keeps operational memory outside the model in BloodHound and its ledger.

SpecterOps introduced Sage, a free AI assistant built into Mythic, a tool used by authorized security testers to see what someone could reach after getting into an organization’s network. Sage can organize information, suggest commands, and help testers follow possible routes to sensitive systems, while normally requiring a person to approve each action. It matters because it could make complex security testing faster and easier to manage, but the company says it is still experimental and should be used only in safe test environments or with explicit permission.

IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics

Kaspersky recorded 1.67 million blocked mobile threats in Q3 2026, with banking Trojans—especially Mamont—and packaged droppers driving much of the malicious-app activity. The quarter also saw AI-enabled Android fraud tools and iOS spyware campaigns exploiting DarkSword through compromised packages and fake App Store apps.

  • 02Trojan-Banker threats accounted for 31.63% of detected malicious mobile apps, and Kaspersky detected 119,688 mobile banking Trojan installation packages.
  • 03Kaspersky identified Android apps that used on-device AI models to interpret fraud commands or search screenshots and gallery images for banking information, including CVV codes.

  • 05iOS campaigns used the DarkSword exploit chain through infected Packagist packages and a fake App Store crypto wallet tracker, with spyware designed to steal data including keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and crypto wallet recovery phrases.

Kaspersky blocked 1,668,368 attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software in Q3 2026, down from 1,996,823 in the previous quarter. It detected 378,456 malicious Android installation packages, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages. Banking Trojans were the leading malicious-app category, representing 31.63% of detected malicious apps, while Mamont variants were the most active banking threats in actual attacks.

The quarter included Android threats that used on-device AI models to interpret commands or examine screenshots and gallery images for banking data such as CVV codes. Attackers also continued packaging banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz into dropper apps, contributing to a sharp rise in that category, while Vo1d proxy Trojans could turn infected devices into internet relay nodes. On iOS, compromised Packagist PHP packages and a fake App Store crypto wallet tracker used the DarkSword exploit chain to deliver spyware that could steal keychain data, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases.

  • Although total mobile-threat detections declined in Q3, the number of detected Android malware samples increased to 378,456, showing that fewer overall alerts did not mean fewer malicious apps were being identified.
  • The sharp increase in Trojan-Dropper detections was linked to criminals packaging known banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz inside delivery apps, while standalone banking Trojans still remained the largest malicious-app category.
  • Vo1d proxy Trojans can turn infected phones into internet relay points, consuming users’ paid data and potentially causing illegal activity or access to banned sites to appear to originate from the victim’s device.
  • The DarkSword campaign selectively loaded its hidden attack component on iOS devices through websites using infected Packagist PHP packages, while also injecting fraudulent casino links into affected sites.
  • The subscription Trojan Subscriber.bh was able to enroll victims in paid services by opening a subscription page invisibly and intercepting the text message containing the confirmation code.

Kaspersky reported that it blocked more than 1.66 million harmful or unwanted mobile-app incidents in the third quarter of 2026, with banking-focused scams making up the largest share. Android users faced fake apps that could steal banking details, sign people up for paid services without their consent, or use their phones’ internet connection for others’ activity, while iPhone users were targeted through infected software packages, a fake wallet-tracking app, and modified apps shared on Telegram. This matters because these schemes can steal money, passwords, private photos and messages, and cryptocurrency recovery phrases, and can even make online activity appear to come from the victim’s phone.

Kaspersky’s Q3 2026 non-mobile threat report recorded more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources, with Web Anti-Virus responding to nearly 47 million unique links. File Anti-Virus blocked 23.7 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects, and 10.88% of users’ computers worldwide encountered at least one local malware threat during the quarter. Ransomware affected 81,556 unique users, while miner attacks affected 217,024 users.

Qilin was the most prolific ransomware group by victims published on data leak sites, accounting for 15.39% of the total, and Kaspersky detected 4,470 new ransomware variants across three new families. The report notes ransomware-linked exploitation of flaws in products including Palo Alto Networks firewall software, SonicWall SMA1000 gateways, Microsoft SharePoint Server and Windows, VMware vCenter, WatchGuard Firebox, and JetBrains TeamCity. It also describes macOS threats delivered through compromised npm, PyPI, and Cargo packages, including stealers and backdoors targeting cryptocurrency wallets, service secrets, configurations, and API keys.

  • Qilin remained the leading ransomware group by victims listed on data leak sites for a second consecutive quarter, accounting for 15.39% of all published victims in Q3 2026.
  • Ransomware variant discovery rose to 4,470 new variants—more than 1.5 times the prior quarter’s count—even as only three new ransomware families were identified.
  • Turkmenistan had the highest reported local-malware exposure at 45.68% of Kaspersky users, while Bangladesh had the greatest web-malware exposure at 12.03%, showing that online and local infection risk were concentrated differently by location.
  • Pakistan accounted for 47.73% of Telnet attacks against Kaspersky IoT honeypots, while Bulgaria’s share of SSH attacks rose nearly fourfold from 5.50% in Q2 to 20.05% in Q3.
  • macOS threats during the quarter included compromised npm, PyPI, and Cargo packages that delivered tools designed to steal wallet data, service secrets, configurations, and API keys.

This report summarizes computer threats seen around the world from July through September 2026, including more than 311 million harmful online attempts and ransomware that locked files for over 81,000 people. Criminal groups such as Qilin continued to pressure victims by publishing stolen data, while attackers also used weaknesses in widely used business software to get into company networks. People and organizations can be affected through infected websites, harmful files, fake software installers, and compromised software updates, putting personal information, business data, and devices at risk.

Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Tracking CopperDragon’s Sparrow Framework Around the Globe

Check Point links three global espionage clusters—SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire—to CopperDragon, a suspected China-nexus malware supplier behind the cross-platform Sparrow framework. The campaigns target telecoms, governments, military, and critical infrastructure using watering holes, compromised Linux servers, credential theft, stealthy kernel capabilities, and new backdoors including SquadC, CopperDoor, and CopperDNS.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Check Point Research identified three operational clusters—SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire—linked by Sparrow malware code similarities and shared infrastructure features across Latin America, Asia, and Europe.
  • 02The researchers track CopperDragon as a possible developer and supplier of the cross-platform Sparrow framework used by China-nexus threat actors including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, and UAT-9244.
  • 03SilentDelivery used compromised government, shipping, and IT or research websites to display fake Chrome certificate warnings and distribute SquadC or SparrowDoor through Trojanized MSI installers.
  • 04OceanGate began by compromising vulnerable internet-facing Linux servers, then used backdoors, Trojanized SSH software, credential theft, and lateral movement into Windows environments before deploying SparrowDoor.
  • 05DarkWire targeted telecommunications providers and government organizations, using CopperDoor and CopperDNS backdoors along with DLL sideloading, proxy tools, and LSASS memory dumping for credential harvesting.

Check Point Research identified three intrusion clusters—SilentDelivery, OceanGate, and DarkWire—targeting high-profile organizations across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. The clusters affected telecommunications providers, government organizations, military entities, research institutions, and critical infrastructure. Researchers linked them through shared infrastructure features and malware similarities in the cross-platform Sparrow framework, and track the possible developer and supplier as CopperDragon. The report notes that shared malware or command-and-control infrastructure does not necessarily establish that separate intrusions were conducted by the same actor.

SilentDelivery used selectively compromised government, shipping, and IT or research websites to show visitors fake Chrome certificate warnings and offer a fraudulent “Certificate Fix” download. The installer deployed the SquadC Windows backdoor or a SparrowDoor variant, while the injected website code used status checks to decide whether to show the fake page and stopped doing so after a successful compromise. OceanGate began by exploiting an internet-facing Linux server, then deployed Linux backdoors, altered SSH components to capture credentials, and later moved into Windows systems using tools for remote access, file inventory, keylogging, and credential collection. Some Sparrow variants also included kernel-level capabilities intended to conceal files, processes, network activity, or backdoor communications.

DarkWire primarily targeted Latin American telecommunications operators and government entities, using CopperDoor and the DNS-tunneling CopperDNS backdoors. Its operators used DLL sideloading to load tools in memory, deployed proxies and an LSASS-dumping module for credential harvesting, and used SMB and WMI for movement across systems. The findings expand visibility into the Sparrow ecosystem and the distinct toolsets and access methods used across the three clusters.

  • SilentDelivery’s injected website code checked a visitor’s IP address and location through repeated requests before showing the fake certificate warning, and it stopped showing the warning after the installed backdoor reported a successful compromise.
  • Some SparrowDoor versions can hide their communications behind a legitimate service on port 443 by intercepting network traffic and redirecting only connections from a specified source IP address to a concealed internal backdoor port.
  • OceanGate operators replaced legitimate SSH client and server components on Linux systems with altered versions that captured administrator credentials, enabling further movement to other Linux hosts.
  • The DarkWire CopperDNS variant used DNS MX queries for command-and-control communications, while its CopperDoor infrastructure used raw TCP wrapped in TLS rather than normal HTTPS.
  • The researchers caution that shared Sparrow malware or command-and-control infrastructure does not by itself prove that separate intrusions were conducted by the same operator.

Researchers found three related spying campaigns that targeted telecommunications companies, government offices, military organizations, research groups, and essential services across Latin America, Asia, and Europe. The attackers used compromised websites and exposed internet systems to trick people into installing fake certificate fixes or to gain entry, then used hidden tools to steal passwords, monitor activity, and move through networks. This matters because access to these organizations could expose sensitive government and operational information and disrupt services that many people rely on.

It provides concrete indicators, newly documented malware and techniques, including watering-hole delivery, Trojanized SSH components, passive port-443 backdoors, DNS tunneling, and LSASS credential dumping.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-89103) SAP Gateway Authentication Bypass via Default Access Control List

SAP Gateway CVE-2026-89103 is a critical pre-authentication authentication bypass that can let network-accessible attackers be treated as internal application servers, potentially enabling unauthorized actions and command execution. Organizations should urgently apply SAP Security Note 3798345, restrict TCP/33NN and TCP/48NN exposure, and replace default gateway ACL rules with explicit secinfo and reginfo controls.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-89103 is a critical SAP Gateway access-control flaw with a CVSS v3.1 score of 10.0 that can allow a network-accessible attacker to be treated as an internal application server before authentication.
  • 02Affected systems include SAP NetWeaver application servers and other SAP kernel-based systems with reachable gateway ports, typically TCP/33NN and TCP/48NN.
  • 03SAP released a kernel update for the issue in SAP Security Note 3798345 during its November 2026 Security Patch Day, and published analysis indicates some older kernels may require the gw/acl_mode_proxy setting after patching.
  • 04The article recommends blocking internet access to SAP Gateway ports, replacing default gateway rules with explicit secinfo and reginfo entries, and monitoring gateway logs for unexpected external program registrations.
  • 05At the time of writing, the vulnerability was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and active exploitation had not been reported.

CVE-2026-89103 is a critical SAP Gateway access-control flaw caused by a default access control list that can classify an external attacker as an internal application server. It has a CVSS v3.1 score of 10.0, requires only network access, and can be exploited before authentication. An attacker accepted in this way could carry out unauthorized actions in the SAP environment, with potentially severe effects on confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

The issue affects SAP NetWeaver application servers and other SAP kernel-based systems with reachable gateway services, commonly on TCP/33NN and TCP/48NN. SAP released a kernel correction in Security Note 3798345, though published analysis indicates older kernels may also require the gw/acl_mode_proxy setting after patching. The article advises organizations to inventory exposed SAP gateways, block internet access to those ports, use explicit secinfo and reginfo rules, and monitor for unexpected external program registrations.

  • A kernel update may not be sufficient by itself, because published analysis indicates older kernels may require the gw/acl_mode_proxy profile parameter to be set after patching.
  • Systems identified through service fingerprinting as SAP NetWeaver should be treated as potentially affected until their actual version and configuration are verified.
  • Public sources disagree on whether the vulnerable condition is the shipped default or depends on missing explicit secinfo and reginfo rules, making direct verification against SAP Security Note 3798345 important.
  • Observed exposure was concentrated in Information Technology and Communication Services, which the article links to service providers and large centrally managed SAP environments with internet-reachable application servers.

The article warns about a serious flaw in SAP Gateway, a component used by SAP business systems, that can let someone on the network pose as a trusted internal system without logging in. It may affect SAP NetWeaver and other SAP systems using certain software versions, especially when their gateway connections are reachable from the internet or other untrusted networks. If abused, the flaw could allow outsiders to take unauthorized actions, access sensitive information, alter systems, or disrupt operations. SAP has released an update, and organizations should also limit outside access to these gateway connections and review their access rules.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a critical, pre-authentication SAP Gateway flaw with a CVSS score of 10.0 and a vendor-issued kernel fix, affecting potentially internet-reachable SAP application servers. Although active exploitation was not reported, the potential for unauthorized actions and command-execution paths makes it broadly important for organizations operating SAP environments.
